title.en: Adam and Eve, the Forbidden Fruit, and Expulsion from Eden
title.zh: 亞當與夏娃的墮落（創世記二至三章）

texts.period: Genesis, c. 6th-5th c. BCE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8001)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 1: Genesis, chapters 2-3, eBook #8001

summary.en: God forms the first man from dust and sets him in a garden in Eden, forbidding him to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil. The serpent persuades the woman that the fruit brings knowledge rather than death; she and her husband eat, are punished with hardship and mortality, and are driven out of Eden, with a flaming sword set to guard the tree of life.
summary.zh: 上帝以塵土造出第一個人，安置在伊甸園中，囑咐他不可吃分辨善惡樹的果子。蛇哄騙女人說果子不會致死，反能開眼如神；她與丈夫吃了，因而受勞苦與死亡的刑罰，被逐出伊甸園，園東有天使與火焰之劍把守生命樹的通路。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrased retellings of the KJV Genesis 2-3 narrative in the collector's own words. The KJV is presented strictly as a public-domain comparative text, not as religious truth. Category 'religious' (canonical scripture + taboo-and-transgression narrative); motifs chosen for the dust-formed Adam and the forbidden-fruit transgression. Coordinates mark a neutral inland spot in southern Mesopotamia, the traditional association for Eden — the location is symbolic, not a verified site.

passages.text: In the second chapter of Genesis the Lord God, having formed a man from the dust of the ground, plants a garden eastward in Eden, full of trees pleasant to see and fit for food, with the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil standing in it. He settles the man there to dress and keep it, warning that he may eat freely of every tree but one: the tree of knowledge, whose fruit brings death on the very day it is eaten. Since it is not good for the man to be alone, God brings every living creature to him to be named, then casts him into a deep sleep, builds a woman out of a rib taken from his side, and the man joyfully recognizes her as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh.

In Genesis 3 the serpent, subtler than every beast of the field, undermines the prohibition: eating will not kill the woman, he insists, but will open her eyes so that she becomes as a god, knowing good and evil. Seeing that the fruit is good for food, lovely to look at, and a path to wisdom, she takes and eats, and gives some to her husband, who eats too. Their eyes are opened, they sew fig leaves into coverings, and they hide among the trees when they hear the Lord God walking in the garden. Judgment follows: the serpent is doomed to crawl and eat dust; the woman is sentenced to sorrowful childbirth under her husband's rule; the man is cursed through a ground that will yield thorns and thistles only under the sweat of his face until he returns to dust. God clothes them in animal skins and drives them out to the east of Eden, where a cherub and a turning, flaming sword seal off the way back to the tree of life.

title.zh: 浪子回頭的比喻（路加福音十五章）

texts.period: Gospel of Luke, c. 80-110 CE; KJV 1611 (Project Gutenberg eBook #8042)

source.work: The Bible, King James version, Book 42: Luke, chapter 15, eBook #8042

summary.en: Jesus tells of a younger son who demands his inheritance, squanders it in a distant country, and returns ruined and repentant, resolving to beg forgiveness. His father runs to meet him, restores him with robe, ring, and a feast, and answers the resentful elder brother that this son who was dead is alive again.
summary.zh: 耶穌講述：小兒子分得家產，遠走他鄉揮霍殆盡，淪為豬倌窮困潦倒，醒悟後回家認罪悔過。父親遠遠望見便奔上前擁抱親吻，為他披袍戴戒、設宴慶祝，並對心生妒忌的長兄說，這兄弟是死而復生、失而復得的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Passages are a paraphrase of the KJV narrative in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: the KJV is treated as a public-domain comparative text only, not as religious truth. Category 'religious' since it is a canonical scripture teaching story; motif 'parable-teaching' reflects the genre. The parable never names a place, so the coordinates are symbolic, on a neutral inland spot near Jerusalem.

passages.text: Jesus tells of a man with two sons. The younger asks for his share of the family property, and having received it, journeys into a far country where he wastes all his money in reckless, riotous living. When a great famine grips the land he falls into poverty and takes a job feeding pigs on a local farm; so hungry is he that he would gladly have filled his belly with the husks the swine eat, and no one gives him anything. Coming to his senses at last, he recalls that even his father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, while he is starving. He resolves to get up, go home, confess that he has sinned against heaven and against his father, and ask to be taken in, no longer as a son, but as one of the hired servants.

While the young man is still a long way off, his father sees him, is moved with compassion, runs to meet him, and falls on his neck with kisses. The son makes his confession, admitting he is no longer worthy to be called a son, but before he can even ask to be made a servant, the father orders his best robe, a ring for his hand, shoes for his feet, and a feast on the fattened calf, declaring that this son of his was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. The elder brother, who has served faithfully for years without ever receiving so much as a feast with his friends, refuses to come in and complains at the celebration. His father answers gently that everything the household owns has always been his, but rejoicing is right, because the boy's brother was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found.

title.en: The Miracles of Saint Bridget of Kildare
title.zh: 聖布里吉德（基爾代爾）的奇蹟

texts.period: Saint's life from 7th c. CE hagiography onward; Baring-Gould, 'Lives of the Saints' (1897, Gutenberg eBook #45604)

source.work: S. Baring-Gould, 'The Lives of the Saints', vol. 2 (February), chapter 'S. Bridget', eBook #45604

summary.en: Baring-Gould recounts the legends of Bridget of Kildare: a wonder-marked birth on a threshold, lavish charity, the founding of her famous double monastery under an oak at Kildare, and miracles such as a cloak thrown over a sunbeam, a spared wolf, and sight restored to a blind nun. Before her death she foretells it, having earlier related a prophetic vision explained by Saint Patrick.
summary.zh: 巴林-古爾德敘述基爾代爾的布里吉德：門檻上誕生的靈異預兆、極度慷慨的童年、在基爾代爾橡樹下建立的修道院，以及斗篷懸擋日光柱、贈狼救農、復明盲修女等奇蹟。她預告自己的死期，此前亦向聖派屈克講出「白田被黑衣耕者翻掘」的異夢，被解為愛爾蘭未來的異端之亂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases written in the collector's own words; Baring-Gould's sentences were not reproduced verbatim. Category 'religious': hagiography (devotional saint-life). Edition caveat: this is the revised 16-volume 1897 edition; the legend source list concedes Bridget's surviving lives are late compositions of uneven reliability, and the cloak-expanding-over-land miracle is not in this edition, so only miracles actually present in this chapter are drawn on. Coordinates point to Kildare town, the account's concrete setting.

passages.text: The legend says Bridget is born on a doorway's threshold, fulfilling a court augury heard before her confinement: happy is the child born neither in the house nor out of it. Her mother, the nobleman Dubtach's slave-girl, has been sold to a bard, but with the bargain that the child is returned to her father; and when the infant is delivered on the threshold, a pitcher of warm milk falls and pours itself over her. Growing up, she gives every beggar whatever he asks, until her exasperated father takes her to the king's court to sell her as too expensive to keep — and when she hands even the royal sword to a beggar, the king refuses to buy a girl ready to give away the king himself. To escape an unwanted suitor she prays for disfigurement and loses an eye; veiled as a nun, she kisses the dry altar-wood, which turns green, and her beauty is restored.

Bridget founds her cell under a great oak at Kildare — 'the cell of the oak' — which grows into a famed double community of monks and nuns in a church divided into three parts. The chapter is crowded with wonders: her priestly charioteer preaching while a loose horse runs free; stolen cows carrying the thieves' tied clothes back to her convent gates; her cloak, thrown in haste over a sunbeam she has mistaken for a beam, holding the ray standing there until midnight; a live wolf delivered into her chariot and offered to the king in place of the one a rustic has killed, sparing the man's life; and the blind nun Dara, whom Bridget heals of darkness only to be asked to shut her eyes again, since a world so visible leaves God less visible to the soul. Bridget relates a vision before Saint Patrick of a white-harvest field torn up by black ploughmen and sowers scattering tares, which Patrick interprets as future false teaching in Ireland. She foretells the hour of her own death, dies on February 1, 525, and her convent keeps its perpetual fire — the 'House of Fire' — burning down to 1220.

region.en: Joseon Korea (Seoul; Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province)
region.zh: 朝鮮王朝（首爾；慶尚道鳥嶺）

texts.period: tale collected by Im Bang (1640-1718); English ed. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales' (1913, Gutenberg eBook #51002)

source.work: Im Pang & Yi Ryuk, tr. James S. Gale, 'Korean Folk Tales: Imps, Ghosts and Fairies' (1913), Tale IV: 'Cheung Puk-chang, the Seer', eBook #51002

summary.en: Cheung Puk-chang is born a marvel of knowledge who needs no study, instantly mastering books, foreign tongues, and the speech of birds and beasts. Loochooan envoys arrive carrying a prophecy that names the day and hour they will meet a Holy Man, and it is fulfilled in him; he also displays distant vision, correctly reporting how a servant is faring far away on his journey.
summary.zh: 崔卜鎮天生異稟，書過目成誦，通天文、醫術、卜算與鳥獸之語。琉球使節攜預言書赴京尋訪「聖人」，其字句在崔卜鎮身上應驗而拜倒；他又能遙視千里，正確指出僕人行踪與遭遇，日期細節日後全部核實。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Gale's translation in the collector's own words; none of Gale's sentences are reproduced verbatim. Category 'myth': a folk wonder-tale of supernatural sight and fulfilled prophecy rather than scripture (per the project genre split). Coordinates use Seoul, where the tale's opening events occur; its farthest episode is at Bird Pass, Kyongsang Province. The Gutenberg text pairs a scholarly historical preamble with each tale; both parts informed the summary.

passages.text: Cheung Puk-chang is a wonder from his earliest years: he needs only to glance through a book once to recite it word for word, and without any study he becomes a master of astronomy, medicine, fortune-telling, music, mathematics, and geomancy. He understands the calls of birds and the voices of beasts, and when he travels with his envoy father to Peking he picks up the language of any strange people after hearing it a single time, astonishing Koreans, Chinese, and foreigners alike. Envoys from Loochoo carry a horoscope-based prophecy in a little book naming the exact year, day, hour, and place they will meet a Holy Man; tracing one envoy station after another, they find him, are struck down with awe, prostrate themselves before him, and are taught at last the Book of Changes in their own tongue. Some call him 'The Mystery.'

One day Cheung Puk-chang calls on his aunt, worried because the servant she sent to do harvest work in Yong-nam County is overdue, and she fears he has met thieves or fire. Puk-chang offers to tell her how matters stand, and gazing off toward the far south he reports that the man is just crossing Bird Pass in Mun-kyong County, Kyong-sang Province — and at that very moment is being beaten by a passing gentleman, since he rode by without dismounting while the official was eating his meal at the top of the hill. The aunt laughs the whole thing off as a joke, but she marks the date on the wall. When the servant arrives on exactly the recorded day, he confirms everything: he was seized by the gentleman's servants, pulled from his horse, and beaten about the face with their straw shoes, precisely as Puk-chang had said.

texts.period: populary legends; F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912, Gutenberg eBook #45723), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji'

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, 'Myths & Legends of Japan' (1912), ch. IX 'Legends of Mount Fuji', eBook #45723

summary.en: Davis's chapter ties Fuji to immortality and apotheosis: the moon-maiden Kaguya commanded that the elixir of life be burned on its peak, and a Chinese emperor who climbs in hope of it dies smiling at the summit. The mountain itself rose in a single night before the woodman Visu; and a goddess of Fuji, a white-clad maiden, healed Yosoji's plague-stricken mother before being carried back to the peak by a cloud.
summary.zh: 戴維斯筆下，富士山與不死傳說相連：輝夜姬命人在峰頂焚燬長生不老藥；中國皇帝登山求藥，卻在山巔含笑而逝；此山一夜拔地而起，出現於樵夫斐素眼前，故稱「不死山」；白衣少女（富士女神）指路取靈泉救瘟疫病母，救人後自化彩雲澨被雲帶回峰頂。

sensitivity.note: Passages are condensed paraphrases of Davis's chapter IX in the collector's own words. Interpretive points: filed as 'myth' (folk legend of a sacred landscape); motifs — Fuji as hallowed peak (sacred-place), the elixir quest (quest-immortality), the cloud-borne apparition of the Goddess of Fuji (theophany). Edition caveat: Davis (1912) is a popular reteller whose versions blend several traditions, and the Kaguya episode is cross-referenced from his chapter III; the passages draw only on chapter IX material. Coordinates are the real Mount Fuji summit area, since the geography here is concrete.

passages.text: Fuji is sacred terrain: pilgrims have climbed it for hundreds of years, its crater was once an active volcano, and its very name is linked with the Aino fire-goddess. Legend even crowns the mountain with the prize of immortality. In the bamboo-cutter romance, the court commanded by the moon-maiden Lady Kaguya ascends Fuji to burn the elixir of life, along with a scroll, upon the peak. The mountain's fame reaches an emperor of China; when he learns that Fuji came into being in a single night, he reasons that so marvelous a mount must yield the elixir of life itself. He gathers handsome youths and maidens and sails to Japan, where the junks ride through a roaring storm before Fuji's white splendour rises before them. Forming his company in procession, the gold-robed emperor walks hour after hour at their head over soft snow, until, eager to be the first to drink, he runs ahead — and his people find him lying on his back, a smile on his face. He has indeed found life eternal, but by way of death.

How Fuji rose: a giant woodman named Visu lives with his family on the then-barren plain of Suruga. One night, as he is about to fall asleep, a sound more terrifying than any thunder comes out of the ground beneath him; fearing an earthquake, he snatches up the younger children and rushes out, to see a great mountain erupting in tongues of flame and dense smoke where there was only flat plain before — a peak that has run unseen under the earth for two hundred miles and leapt up in a single night. Spellbound, Visu watches dawn dress the mountain in opal, and names it Fuji-yama, the Never-Dying Mountain, its seeming eternity giving rise to the old belief in an elixir hidden upon it.

Another tale casts the mountain as a living healer: Yosoji, whose mother is dying of smallpox, is sent by the magician Kamo Yamakiko to fetch water from Fuji's south-west slope; a lady in white guides him to the stream by the shrine of the God of Long Breath. After five visits his mother and many villagers are cured; but when Yosoji returns to give thanks the shrine has dried up, and the maiden — she is the Goddess of Fuji — refuses all thanks, swings her camellia branch into the air to summon a cloud from the sacred peak, and lets it carry her home.
